title: Bellarmino reconciles bold verbs: ‘save me / give me’ mean by praying and merits, not as author
source_text: LVI. Ut autem istas preces, & plures alias similes, quae sunt in Ecclesia Romanae usitate, Bellarminus cum supra posita doctrina conciliet, notat, quum dixit, non debere peti a Sanctis, nisi ut orent pro nobis, se non agere de verbis, sed de sensu verborum. Nam quantum ad verba, inquit, licet dicere, Sancte Petre miserere mei, Salva me, aperi mihi aditum caeli: item Da mihi sanitatem corporis, da patientiam, da mihi fortitudinem, &c. dummodo intelligamus, salva me, & miserere mei, orando pro me; Da mihi hoc, & illud tuis precibus & meritis. De Sanctor. Beatitudine lib. 1. cap. 17.
pass_a_gloss: But that Bellarmine may reconcile those prayers, and many other similar ones which are customary in the Roman Church, with the doctrine set down above, he notes that when he said that nothing ought to be asked of the Saints except that they pray for us, he is not dealing with the words but with the sense of the words. For as to the words, he says, it is lawful to say, Saint Peter have mercy on me, Save me, open to me the entrance of heaven: likewise Give me health of body, give patience, give me fortitude, etc.—provided we understand, save me and have mercy on me, by praying for me; Give me this and that by thy prayers and merits. On the Beatitude of the Saints, book 1, chapter 17.
pass_b_english: Bellarmino: the ban is on sense, not wording.
You may say ‘Save me / Give me’ to a Saint if you mean by his prayers and merits—not as author of the gift.
